items._ogDesc: In Maine, a border state that has been hit hard by the Canada-U.S. trade war, incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins is hoping to hold off Democrat challenger Troy Jackson.
items.body:
As Americans head to the polls for midterm elections Tuesday, the outcome could have significant consequences for Canada. CTVNews.ca will have live results, breaking updates, real-time election data and on-the-ground reporting from key battleground states.

Maine voter Sydney Olson says she doesn’t get why the United States is waging a trade war with Canada.

“There’s hardly any Americans who want Canadians to be antagonized and want to be in a trade war with Canada,” Olson said outside a polling station in Bangor, Maine.

“We have no problem with Canada. We love Canada. Why bother?”

Olson said she voted for Maine’s Democratic candidate for Senate in a race that could decide if U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republicans continue to control the chamber.

In Maine, a border state that has been hit hard by the Canada-U.S. trade war, incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins is hoping to hold off Democrat challenger Troy Jackson.

Michael Furrow, a retired military officer, said he voted for Collins because of her ability to get federal backing for projects critical to Maine’s economy.

But the 23-year Maine resident said he also wants to see an end to Trump’s tariffs on Canadian imports.

“Trade needs to be open and free across the border,” Furrow said outside the arena where he voted Tuesday.

“We got two great countries. Work together and I think we can do wonderful things.”

The economic impact of the trade war has become a key obstacle for Collins, who has asked Maine voters to return her to the upper chamber of Congress for a sixth term.

Polling shows many voters in Maine are unhappy with Trump policies that have pushed up energy prices and caused Canadian tourism to plummet.

Many of those who spoke to The Canadian Press on Tuesday hoped for an end to the tariff skirmish between the two countries that Trump started after coming into office last year.

“Canada’s our friend and neighbour. Why should we be treating them like we’re treating them?” Dan O’Connell asked as he headed into a polling station in Brewer, Maine.

While he voted for Collins in the past, O’Connell said this year he was ready to back her opponent, in part so that a Democrat-controlled Senate could rein in Trump’s tariffs.

But some Republican voters said Tuesday they hope the levies on Canadian imports remain, at least to some extent.

“I don’t want to see them gone but I’d like to see a level playing field,” Mark McPherson said after marking his ballot for Collins.

McPherson said he agreed with Trump’s claim that the U.S. has been “ripped off” through global trade.

A few voters had Canada on their minds on Tuesday.

Donna Twombly, who was born in Maine, said her grandparents were Danish citizens who immigrated to Canada before settling in the U.S.

Twombly said she was angry when Trump imposed his first wave of levies on Canada and other countries last year.

“I went out and bought a Canadian flag,” she said. “I only found a small one when I went shopping but I put it up on my home.”

Maine, a Northeastern U.S. state bordering both Quebec and New Brunswick by land, relies heavily on Canadian trade.

Federal government figures show the state imports $4.1 billion in goods from Canada each year, making it Maine’s largest trading partner.

That includes $2 billion in heating oil, more than half a billion dollars in forestry products and $263 million in electricity from New Brunswick.

In a column published earlier this year, Maine Gov. Janet Mills said the state’s forest product exports to Canada have dropped by 20 per cent since Trump started his trade war, causing job losses.

The number of trips by Canadians to Maine dipped sharply last year, according to an analysis of border data by the Maine Center for Economic Policy.

U.S. tariffs have strained New Brunswick’s forestry sector and manufacturing base and has cut into the bottom lines of breweries.

But politics watchers say it’s not clear which result would offer a win for Canada, or if a win is even likely.

Collins has pitched herself as an independent who isn’t afraid of breaking with her party and voting against Trump on tariffs she has long opposed.

Jackson, meanwhile, says Collins hasn’t done enough as a Republican to push back against the levies that have disrupted Maine’s forestry, seafood and tourism industries.

At a debate last month, Collins said she successfully lobbied the White House to get Canadian concrete, pulp and road salt removed from the tariff list.

Jackson snapped back, saying, “We can’t eat road salt.”

The exchange went viral and spurred the exchange of “let them eat road salt” memes among progressives.

Then, with less than two weeks before the midterm elections, Collins announced the U.S. was lifting tariffs on nine categories of Canadian goods she said are crucial to Maine’s hard-hit agricultural industries.

It was seen as an attempt by Trump — who has not campaigned in Maine this election cycle — to help Collins keep her seat.

But in the same executive order lifting some tariffs, Trump imposed new levies on dozens of new categories such as cocoa powder, paints and varnishes, shampoos, vinyl flooring, archery equipment and carpets.

Lori Turnbull, a political-science professor at Dalhousie University, says there isn’t a way for Canada to win despite being at least partly on the ballot in Maine.

Turnbull noted Trump relies on his presidential powers to impose tariffs, going around the legislative branch of the U.S. government.

“I don’t think that any midterm outcome is a guaranteed win for Canada. I think we could still get screwed either way,” she said by phone.

Trump’s levies on a swath of countries triggered retaliatory tariffs by Ottawa and a trade war that has damaged industries and raised costs on both sides of the border.

The previous round of trade talks between the two sides broke down in August, but Trump claimed Sunday that Canada and the United States are “very close” to reaching a trade deal.

Trump told reporters the two countries have a “concept of a very good deal” that would be great for America, American farmers and Canada.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said on social media that he’d had a “good conversation” with Trump on the future of trade.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

With files from Kelly Geraldine Malone and The Associated Press

Eli Ridder, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says “more intense” trade negotiations with the United States have started since his call with President Donald Trump last weekend.
items.body:
ST JOHN’S — Prime Minister Mark Carney says “more intense” trade negotiations with the United States have started since his call with President Donald Trump last weekend.

“We’ve made progress but we haven’t finished,” Carney told reporters Tuesday in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda.

Carney said some of Canada’s “red lines” have been taken off the table, including language, culture and Canada’s ability to negotiate trade deals with other markets.

“They’re asking less and they’re offering more but we’re not quite there,” he said.

Trump told Fox News in an interview Tuesday that a deal with Canada is imminent.

“Canada is very good, we’re going to make a deal with Canada very soon. We’re going to make ⁠a great deal,” he said.

He also claimed Canada would provide fertilizer to the United States tariff-free. Canada does not charge any export tariffs on fertilizer or its components, including potash.

Carney called off formal trade talks with the United States in August at the eleventh hour as the two sides worked to finalize a deal before a new round of U.S. tariffs was imposed on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The prime minister said Tuesday there are still important issues that need to see progress in negotiations but didn’t say what those are. He also did not say when Canada’s chief negotiator is likely to return to Washington.

“Because we have made progress, it was felt (to be) important to acknowledge that publicly,” he said. “It’s not always necessary to have the trade negotiators go in formally into the U.S. trade representative’s offices or the Department of Commerce.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026

With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

items.body:
Industrial conglomerate 3M said on Tuesday it would commit nearly US$7.35 billion over nine years to settle PFAS “forever chemicals”-related personal injury claims.

PFAS are a group of manufactured chemicals used in products resistant to heat, stains, grease and water. They have been linked to health issues including liver damage, lower birth weight, reduced antibody response to vaccines, and kidney and testicular cancer.

3M, which is facing thousands of lawsuits over PFAS contamination, did not admit liability and said it was prepared to continue to defend itself in litigation.

The settlement addresses about 99 per cent of current personal-injury claims inside and outside the Aqueous Film-Forming Foam Multi-District Litigation (AFFF MDL). About 115,000 to 120,000 plaintiffs are eligible to participate, according to the company.

The payment structure includes a US$50 million payment in 2026 and no payments in 2027, with about 20 per cent of payments due in the final two years.

3M expects to record a pre-tax charge of US$5.8 billion in the fourth quarter, adding that the charge would not impact its previously issued forecast.

“This settlement is a significant milestone for 3M and substantially reduces litigation uncertainty,” CEO William Brown said in a statement on Tuesday.

The conglomerate said all remaining and future personal-injury claims, both inside and outside the AFFF MDL, would be managed through several settlement mechanisms.

In 2023, 3M reached a US$10.3 billion settlement with a host of U.S. public water systems to resolve water pollution claims tied to “forever chemicals.”

Many other companies, including DuPont and Corteva, Chemours are facing lawsuits related to PFAS.

3M said on Tuesday it has successfully completed its previously announced plan to discontinue the manufacture of all PFAS globally by the end of 2025.

(Reporting by Anshuman Tripathy and Vallari Srivastava in Bengaluru; Editing by Rashmi Aich and Sherry Jacob-Phillips)

items._ogDesc: Americans are casting their votes Tuesday in U.S. midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s chaotic and controversial second term.
items.body:
As Americans head to the polls for midterm elections Tuesday, the outcome could have significant consequences for Canada. CTVNews.ca will have live results, breaking updates, real-time election data and on-the-ground reporting from key battleground states.

DETROIT — Americans are casting their votes Tuesday in U.S. midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s chaotic and controversial second term.

The outcome will decide which party controls Congress and whether there will be a check on Trump’s unprecedented use of executive power over the remainder of his time in office.

“For this country to work at its best, citizens need to be involved,” said 49-year-old Andrew Harris, who cast ballots for Democrats in Birmingham, Mich. “And there’s no better way to be involved than to be a voter, an informed voter. It’s a very important day.”

Republicans have been on defence throughout this turbulent midterm campaign season, with polls showing Trump’s approval plummeting due to rising gas and diesel prices, high inflation and the unpopular war with Iran.

Trump made his closing arguments of the campaign Monday. He defended his administration’s tariffs and policies and claimed his second term has seen the “best” economy ever, despite widespread voter disapproval of his handling of pocketbook issues.

Trump also denigrated Democrats, calling their party extreme and dangerous and claiming they hate America.

Democrats have faced controversies of their own, including a shocking eleventh-hour party fracture in a tight Michigan Senate race. Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

Alan Latham, a 44-year-old attorney and lifelong Michigander, said he was worried about affordability but was more motivated to back a candidate who promises progress instead of polarization.

“For me the candidate that’s going to push forward us in a positive direction as a country, as a people, unify us, is what really brought me out to the polls and what really is important to me as a voter and as a citizen,” Latham said after casting a ballot in White Lake for El-Sayed.

At the same polling station, Mark Pospisil, 43, said he’s pretty neutral on a lot of political issues. Pospisil said he voted for Rogers because the Republican would “honour and fear God and be best to implement good laws for our community.”

Polling shows Democrats are close to taking the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a narrow majority.

Control of the Senate is much less clear and the Michigan race could prove critical to Democrats’ chances of securing the net gain of four seats they need for a majority.

To control the Senate, Democrats likely need to win seats in places like Maine and Alaska, where Trump’s unpopular trade war with Canada has become a ballot box issue.

Trump recently made changes to 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods to offer a reprieve to industries hit hard in Maine, a border state where longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces a tough contest.

Mary Monroe, casting her ballot in Bangor, Maine, said while it’s important to be friendly with your neighbours, “I don’t think the United States should be taken advantage of.”

At the same polling station, Tyler Levesque said, “Canada is our partner.”

“It’s not fair to us as Mainers, as a community, to suffer because of failed economic policy,” Levesque said.

While the trade war with Canada may not have been the top issue on voters’ minds in border states, the cost of living is definitely driving voting intentions. Many Americans are angered by Trump’s policies, which have driven up costs at gas stations and grocery stores.

Trump returned to the White House after promising to boost the economy, reduce inflation and keep the United States out of foreign wars. He made gains among young men, the Hispanic community and Black men based on those pledges.

Halfway through his second term, many of those same voters say they feel duped.

Dylan Raford supported Trump in 2024 — even though he was too young at the time to vote — and hyped up the president to family and friends. The 19-year-old described himself as a business owner, entrepreneur and “big free market type of guy.”

Raford said he now feels betrayed.

“I did like Trump. I did. As a Black person, I got so much hate for it,” Raford said.

“He made me a fool. He made all those people right.”

Like many voters who turned out for Trump in 2024, Raford doesn’t have a party affiliation. He said he’s voting Democrat in the South Carolina midterm races because he wants Trump to face restraints.

The Senate race for Lindsey Graham’s old seat in historically red South Carolina has turned out to be a surprise battleground. Many voters have criticized Trump’s endorsement of Darline Graham Nordone to run for her late brother’s seat, citing her lack of experience and multiple fumbles on the campaign trail.

But a blue wave — which would solidify Trump as a lame duck president — is not guaranteed. Many Republicans remained determined and organized ahead of the vote.

Jay Jamil, with Chaldean Association Iraqi Catholics in Michigan, said his community was motivated to get out the vote for Rogers because the Republican would be good for local businesses and families.

“Mike Rogers has filled the Chaldean need list. What they asked him for, he helped them,” Jamil said.

With files from Eli Ridder in Bangor, Maine and The Associated Press

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Organigram Global Inc. has signed a deal to buy Aurora Cannabis Inc. in an agreement that values the company at $561 million.
items.body:
TORONTO — TORONTO — Organigram Global Inc. has signed a deal to buy Aurora Cannabis Inc. in an agreement that values the company at $561 million, after a hostile offer from Curaleaf was rebuffed earlier this year.

Organigram CEO James Yamanaka said the transaction is a defining step in the company’s strategy to build a disciplined, global cannabis leader.

“By bringing together Aurora’s established global medical cannabis platform with our Canadian operations and growing international footprint, we are creating a larger, stronger, and more diversified company,” he said in a news release Tuesday.

Under the offer, Aurora shareholders have the option to receive $7.80 per share in cash, 5.8626 Organigram shares per share or a combination. The total cash available is capped at $253.6 million, while the number of shares available under the offer is limited to 205.8 million.

The transaction has received unanimous support from the board of directors at both firms. The companies said the deal represents a 93 per cent premium to Aurora’s share price as of Aug. 10 and a 21 per cent premium to the implied value of the Curaleaf offer, which was amended on Oct. 6.

Aurora executive chair and CEO Miguel Martin said the offer is the result of a robust strategic review process and delivers compelling value.

“Combining with Organigram will accelerate Aurora’s international growth strategy by strengthening commercial execution, expanding our product and (research and development) capabilities, and extending our global operating network,” he said.

The deal comes after Curaleaf Holdings Inc. made a hostile offer for Aurora earlier this year.

Stamford, Conn.-based Curaleaf took its offer directly to shareholders in August after it said Aurora’s board refused to engage in discussions. Aurora said at the time it would consider the offer and was forming a special committee to mull the unsolicited bid.

In September, Aurora urged shareholders to reject the hostile takeover bid, saying it undervalued Aurora and was not in the best interest of shareholders.

Curaleaf sweetened the deal in October, making an offer valued at US$5 per Aurora share, based on Curaleaf’s Oct. 2 closing share price. The proposal included 0.4013 Curaleaf shares plus US$1 cash for each Aurora share.

Its previous offer had included paying Aurora shareholders US$4.00 per share, plus US$0.75 cash for each Aurora share.

In a statement issued Tuesday evening, Curaleaf said its enhanced Oct. 6 bid for Aurora remains outstanding.

“Curaleaf believes its offer represents better value, offering a superior combined business with a stronger capital markets profile, greater certainty and speed to close, and greater anticipated synergies,” the statement said.

“Curaleaf will study Organigram’s alternative transaction and awaits disclosure of material details which have not been provided, including any break fee, management and board composition going forward, and any investor rights being granted to BAT. It is also revealing that neither Aurora nor Organigram made any reference to whether the transaction is dilutive or accretive to shareholders.”

Organigram and Aurora said the transaction would bring about several benefits.

This includes bringing together complementary operations, including Aurora’s manufacturing capacity, pharmacy and patient network with Organigram’s Canadian recreational brands and European footprint.

The companies said the deal would create more than $50 million in synergies from cross-selling, procurement scale and other factors. The deal would also allow for greater scale and better supply chains.

The deal is expected to close in January 2027 and is subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals as well as permission from the Supreme Court of British Columbia.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

The post The Data Center Boom: Internet Landlords & A $3 Trillion Real Estate Bubble appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: The scramble to build data centers isn't about AI, it's a $3 trillion real estate bubble as firms fight to become landlords of the internet.
items.body:
The AI revolution requires an unprecedented build-out of data centers. At least, that’s how the narrative goes. A quick peek at the data reveals a funny detail—most aren’t being built. An energy shortage? Nah, most don’t even apply for a connection to the power grid. This is about a little tax code change that sparked a stampede to become landlords of the internet. A multi-trillion dollar speculative bubble, complete with flippers. Seriously.

The Scramble To Build Data Centers

A scramble to build data centers is a bit of an understatement. In Canada, over 200 data centers have been announced or are in development. That includes 159 hyperscale facilities—those with at least 50 megawatts (MW) of capacity. Out of those, 116 are planning for over 100 MW of capacity. That’s a big jump from the 5 hyperscale facilities in Canada today.

The US is seeing a much bigger boom. Vancouver-based Aterio tracks 8,434 data centers, from announcement to operations. Their data shows 2,145 in operation, 888 under construction, and 4,442 announced. “The remaining 959 are delayed, land banked, not approved or cancelled, which we keep tracking because they often come back,” notes the predictive analytics firm.

If that seems unrealistic, wait until you crunch some numbers.

Data Center Energy Math Doesn’t Add Up

Big numbers are hard to appreciate, so let’s make them relatable. The average home in Canada and the US uses ~11,000 kilowatt hours (kWh) of electricity per year, about 1.25 kilowatts (kW). A megawatt (MW) is 1,000 kW, equal to the power draw of ~800 households. A gigawatt (GW) is 1,000,000 kW or 1,000 MW, equal to the power draw of ~800,000 households. Easy peasy, right?

Now let’s apply that. Canada’s 116 hyperscalers that need a minimum of 100 MW need 11.6 GW of power. That’s equal to the power of roughly 9.28 million households in a country with only ~16.85 million households. Canada’s Minister of Artificial Intelligence stated there are 20 GW in the pipeline.

Just 750 large projects in the US will be using 45 GW of additional power, equal to 36 million households. That’s a lot of automated Realtor emails for our spam boxes.

Does that sound a little unrealistic? Canada’s government seems to agree. When asked about the AI minister’s 20 GW claim, officials didn’t just concede it was an exaggeration. They outright stated, “most of this proposed capacity is not expected to proceed.”

Oh, cool. Wait… what? We’ll circle back, but first, let’s talk about the scramble to become landlords of the internet. That’s not me being cute. It’s in your tax code.

The Scramble To Become Landlords of The Internet

The internet is synonymous with giants like Google and Meta, but they’re mostly tenants. They’re now building data centers, but for the most part, they pay rent to “internet landlords,” a term coined by University of Maryland Associate Professor Daniel Greene.

“A tremendous amount of money and innovation may go into Google’s advertising networks, but those networks are largely housed in cages rented from a third party,” he explains.

He argues that internet landlords extract rent through three primary asset types: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) for public network peering, co-location facilities where tenants rent space and server bandwidth, and managed storage. Internet companies may build products, but they have to rent infrastructure to get it to you.

One Weird Tax Trick That Ruined The Internet

This isn’t a happy accident but a long battle that only ended in 2016, which is why you’re hearing about it now. “To secure their status as [Real Estate Investment Trusts] REITs, internet landlords had to prove that the internet was a physical place you could own, manage, and lease, like an apartment building or a storage unit,” explains Greene.

IRS Private Letter Rulings (PLRs) from 2007 to 2014 helped to close gaps, including classifying payments as “rent.” The idea took off in 2015 after a PLR cleared the way for data center Equinix to become a Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT). Congress then codified the rules with the PATH Act (2015), and the IRS in 2016. Data centers were fully cleared to become tax-advantaged, globally traded, liquid financial assets.

What’s so important about being a REIT? Until the 1960s, real estate was incredibly illiquid, reducing its value. To stimulate investment, REITs became eligible for a pass-through structure. Corporate profits are usually subject to “double taxation.” They pay income taxes on net profits, and then they can pay out dividends from the profits. Investors then pay their own income taxes on that additional income. REITs distribute virtually the entire net profit as dividends, and investors pay income taxes on that income.

Roughly 10 years ago, the internet’s landlords secured the same treatment. It’s relatively new, which is why you’re only recently hearing about it. That and the recent rush to target retail investors with IPOs, such as Brookfield’s Csquare and Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC), the latter being a REIT itself.

On that note, let’s circle back to those data centers that are very unlikely.

Nearly 5 Data Centers Announced For Each Built & Braggawatts

The announcements (and debt) to build data centers are booming, but the building—not so much. In Canada, only 1 of 8 hyperscale facilities slated for a 2027 launch has actually broken ground. JP Morgan recently warned that over 60% of US data center capacity for 2027 hasn’t broken ground. Nearly 5 data centers are announced for every one built. That’s excluding cancelled projects.

The media widely attributes the delays to NIMBYs, who don’t want to share their energy. However, most data centers haven’t even asked for energy. A recent study of 252 active US data center announcements found 129 had no utility filings, SEC disclosures, or issued permits. That’s like announcing you’re going to bake a cake, but don’t have flour, sugar, an oven, or a kitchen.

Unproven and exaggerated data centers are so common that the industry has a term—braggawatts. These are, um, inspirational announcements with virtually zero chance of being built. “The amount of power, and even the amount of financing required to meet these upper end projections, it doesn’t exist,” explained Chris Sharp, CTO at Digital Realty, the firm that pioneered data REITs in 2004.

Sharp warns that developers are increasingly entering the space and overstating their abilities. Raw land of that scale is expensive. The cost to build out a hyperscale is almost unimaginable to most. Lucky for the speculators, they don’t need to build it if they can flip it first.

Data Center Flippers

Is it really a real estate bubble without flippers? A whopping 72% of US AI data center power requests are phantom loads. Phantom loads are speculative requests that require utility companies to set aside dedicated power. The artificial shortage pushes energy prices higher, but improves the project value. The flipper may not have the funds to build it out, but institutions that need to allocate investor funds do.

The problem isn’t going unnoticed. In Canada, B.C. Hydro now requires C$25k per MW in bid security, or C$2.5 million per 100 MW facility. Fail to build by the deadline, the funds are forfeited. It’s a little light in contrast to what’s emerging in the US.

Earlier this year, Texas adopted a US$100k study fee plus a deposit of US$50k per MW. A deposit of US$5 million is a sign of a pretty strong commitment. Though Ohio has the toughest test we’ve come across. Applicants pay US$10k-US$100k per load study, and 85% of contracted capacity for 12 years, even if less is used.

The scale of debt in the pipeline suggests that it may be an underreaction. Canada’s financing is more opaque, but experts have noted that debt raises “start at several hundred million dollars and exceed well over a billion dollars.” Though that’s chump change compared to the mounting liabilities in the US.

US data centers and related infrastructure are tied to US$1.3 trillion in debt, according to Atrium. Morgan Stanley also estimates a US$1.5 trillion “gap” in financing for data centers through 2028. Only the equivalent of Canada’s GDP? I guess we all have to tighten our purse strings in this economy.

AI has hit an inflection point, and that means more infrastructure is needed. But technological revolution and a bubble aren’t mutually exclusive. The internet was revolutionary, but that didn’t stop the Dot Com bubble. AI isn’t different—it’s just wrapped around a real estate bubble and cushioned by more tax dollars.

As Americans head to the polls for midterm elections Tuesday, the outcome could have significant consequences for Canada. CTVNews.ca will have live results, breaking updates, real-time election data and on-the-ground reporting from key battleground states.

Featuring one of the most diverse slates of both Democratic and Republican candidates in recent years, this midterm election has set up a possible wave of historic leadership firsts across the country.

Voters on Tuesday could propel into office the first Indigenous female governor and Indigenous women senators, the first Black female governor, the first openly gay U.S. senator and the first Muslim U.S. senator, among other milestones. Most are Democrats, but the GOP could also break ground.

While some of these candidates have avoided focusing on the inherent historic value of their race, gender, religion or sexual orientation, some voters’ rights advocates are celebrating how the electorate has expanded.

“These firsts show how our country is changing,” Alexis Anderson-Reed, president and CEO of State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity in democracy, said via e-mail.

“For years, people of color and LGBTQ+ communities have organized, knocked on doors, talked to voters, held conversations, and done the hard work of saving our democracy,” Anderson-Reed said. ”These wins are because of them.”

Here are some of the races where history could be made:

First Indigenous female governor

Democrat Deb Haaland already broke barriers in 2018 as one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress. Then she became the first Native American cabinet secretary, running former U.S. president Joe Biden’s Department of the Interior. Charles Curtis, from the Kaw Nation, was former U.S president Herbert Hoover’s vice president.

Now the Laguna Pueblo citizen is poised to add first Indigenous woman governor to the list if she beats Republican Gregg Hull, a former mayor, in New Mexico.

Oklahoma is the only state to elect a tribal citizen for governor — Democrat Johnston Murray in the 1950s and current Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt.

Haaland shrugged off a question about her various political identities in a recent interview with The Associated Press.

“I mean, somebody has to be the first,” she said. “I just don’t want to be the last, right?”

But she says she’s proud to see how Indigenous people care about representation as other Indigenous women run. “It truly does matter,” Haaland said. “It’s not just a slogan.”

First Indigenous woman senators

Mary Peltola, who is Yup’ik and a Democrat, was considered a trailblazer in 2022 when she became the first Indigenous Alaskan elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. Now the former congresswoman is trying to do the same in the Senate by unseating Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The honour could also go to Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive Democrat and a citizen of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe who faces Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter.

And if Tafoya wins, she too would make history — as the first Republican of Latina heritage to sit in the U.S. Senate.

First Black female governor

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Lisa Demuth could end a 250-year streak without a Black woman serving as a state’s governor.

Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, is running against Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman, to be governor of Georgia. If she wins, Bottoms would also be Georgia’s first governor of colour. All 83 of Georgia’s previous governors have been white men.

Demuth, the former Minnesota House speaker, is going up against longtime Minnesota U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar. Whatever the outcome, Minnesota will get its first female governor.

Stacey Abrams is the only Black woman to come close to winning a governor’s race when she got the Georgia Democratic Party’s nomination in 2018 and 2022.

First Muslim U.S. senator

Abdul El-Sayed could be the first Muslim American to serve in the U.S. Senate.

The progressive Michigan Democrat needs to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in what has been a very tight and contentious race.

El-Sayed has had to contend with Republicans all the way up to Trump implying or overtly stating that the Michigan-born epidemiologist is not American and supports terrorism. Trump has called him “dangerously radical,” “too extreme” and referred to him as “Mohammed.” El-Sayed and his supporters have denounced the attacks as Islamophobic or racist affronts to religious freedom.

First openly gay U.S. senator

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas could be the U.S.’ first openly gay senator if he’s elected in New Hampshire. He is running against former Republican U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu.

Pappas already became the first openly gay member of Congress when he was elected in 2018.

This potential new benchmark is not something Pappas has dwelled on while campaigning, saying “I’m not running to make history.” But he also applauded the fact that his sexual orientation was not a huge source of discussion among potential voters.

First Black governors

The U.S. could go from having only three elected Black governors in its 250-year history to gaining seven more overnight.

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, the third one in the U.S. and the only current Black governor, is projected to win re-election. Besides Georgia and Minnesota, he could also have new peers in Florida, Wisconsin, Nevada, South Carolina and Michigan.

Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, has called the presence of so many Black gubernatorial contenders “a unique moment.” It’s not “an applause line” but a challenge to make diverse gubernatorial nominees more common, he said.

Record year of women running for governor and Congress

This midterm has been a record-breaker for women vying for state and federal offices. Democrats increased their 2022 number of women candidates to 19 running for governor, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. The Republican Party has seven women setting their sights on governor.

Like Minnesota, Tennessee will elect its first female governor. The main candidates are Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn and Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis city councilwoman.

The election of the first Democratic Asian American woman as governor could happen in Vermont with Amanda Janoo, who is half Malaysian, or Oklahoma with Cyndi Munson, a former state lawmaker of Korean descent. Former Republican Gov. Nikki Haley of South Carolina, who is of Indian heritage, was the first Asian American female governor.

Nearly 300 women, including incumbents, are running for the U.S. Senate and House, as documented by Rutgers’ Center for American Women and Politics.

Among them is Democrat Juliana Stratton in Illinois. If Stratton, who is Black, wins her Senate race, then she and fellow Democrat Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who is of Thai heritage, will make Illinois the first state to be represented by two female senators of colour.

Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, and Savannah Peters in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed to this report.

items.title: Why alt lending is no longer the last resort for brokers
items.description: Top lenders at MortgageFest Canada say alt lending is now the prime solution for many Canadians
items.content: <p>Top lenders at MortgageFest Canada say alt lending is now the prime solution for many Canadians</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0000_639293283152242730.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Top lenders at MortgageFest Canada say alt lending is now the prime solution for many Canadians
items.body:
The image of alternative lending as a short-term fix for borrowers with damaged credit has, by most measures, run its course.

At MortgageFest Canada, held at Mississauga’s International Centre, senior executives from four of the country’s leading alt lenders made a straightforward argument: the channel has matured into a primary solution for a wide and growing share of the Canadian borrower base, and brokers who continue to treat it as a backup option are forgoing significant business.

“The alternative space is part of your prime option now,” said Cam DelliPizzi, regional sales director at MCAN Financial.

“It’s as simple as that. And if you’re not thinking about it that way, you’re losing opportunity for yourself.”

A borrower profile that no longer fits a single box

The shift is structural, not cyclical. As qualification criteria at Canada’s major chartered banks have narrowed under regulatory pressure, a growing range of creditworthy clients — self-employed borrowers, entrepreneurs, holders of multiple investment properties, and those navigating divorce or Canada Revenue Agency obligations — have landed in the alternative channel not because of damaged credit, but because of how banks define qualifying income.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthONE Bank of Canada, offered a data point that reframes the conversation: the average FICO score among his institution’s alternative borrowers sits at 763. That's a number that, he noted, outperforms some Big Six portfolios in certain segments.

“Banks have very, very specific ways of looking at income,” Armstrong said.

“That’s where the alternative lenders can come in and have a different risk appetite — to be able to say, we want to look at that cash flow of the business. Some of our clients have multiple properties — bank statement approach, investment properties, holdcos — stuff that’s just a little bit outside of what the traditional bank is.”

Joel Cote, chief operating officer at Haventree Bank, described the evolution as a reclassification rather than a demotion.

“It’s no longer, for many, a short-term solution,” he said.

“For many clients that fit this profile, the alt solution is the prime solution.”

As Canadian mortgage debt continues to swell past record levels, the proportion of borrowers whose income structures fall outside conventional bank parameters is only expected to grow.

Packaging files and building lender relationships

For Prakash Bector, vice president of sales and distribution at EQ Bank, the sharpest opportunity for brokers in the alt space lies in how they prepare and present files.

For self-employed clients in particular, income verification requires understanding the full shape of the business — revenue, overhead, how the client structures expenses — not just a line-15 figure.

“The more equipped you are upfront, the easier it’s going to be for all of us to be able to assess the deal and give you a quick answer and move the file along,” he said.

The panelists were united on one practical step that few brokers take: call the lender’s business development manager and ask directly how income is calculated.

Armstrong noted that of more than 100 brokers in the room, fewer than 2% had done so. That single conversation, he argued, can redefine a broker’s performance in the alt space.

Brokers looking to sharpen their edge with alternative lenders would do well to start there.

“Build the package for the lender,” he said. “If you build it for yourself, it doesn’t help the lender.”

Cote offered a clear summary of what separates approvals from declines.

“What kills deals are surprises,” he said. “The more info that we know upfront, the better equipped we are to try to navigate a solution.”

As artificial intelligence begins reshaping how mortgage brokers handle file complexity and client communication, the ability to build clean, transparent files quickly is only going to matter more.

items.title: Return-to-office trend poses new challenges for Canadian homebuyers
items.description: Lenders expect clarity on a borrower’s arrangement with their employer as companies ramp up expectations for in-office work
items.content: <p>Lenders expect clarity on a borrower’s arrangement with their employer as companies ramp up expectations for in-office work</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639293254820279869.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lenders expect clarity on a borrower’s arrangement with their employer as companies ramp up expectations for in-office work
items.body:
A major pandemic-era trend was the movement of Canadians further away from their office location as remote-working arrangements became more and more prominent, helping facilitate migration into more affordable markets.

But a gradual ramping-up of return-to-office efforts by employers is raising questions about the future of that movement – and whether lenders will take a more rigorous approach to mortgage applicants who live far from their workplace.

Lenders are still generally receptive to borrowers living a long way from their workplace, but Durham Region-based mortgage broker Sherry Corbitt told Canadian Mortgage Professional that further clarification or assurance from employers about that arrangement remains commonplace.

“A lot of the times we’ll send in the job letter and the paystub, and then we’ll get back, ‘Please revise the job letter to say that there’s a hybrid, or what the obligation of in-office is,’” she said. “I would probably say I see that on half of my purchase files.”

A recent survey by real estate giant RE/MAX Canada showed a growing number of Canadians are prepared to make compromises to buy a property, including moving further away from their current location.

But Corbitt said lenders generally want answers as soon as a commute stretches beyond 100 kilometres. “They want to understand, ‘Does this client really plan to do a three-hour commute in the winter, or can they work from home?’ If it’s work from home, it’s checked and gone – the condition is waived,” she said.

“If it’s no, you have to commute for three hours, they start saying: ‘Well, are they paying rent somewhere? Are they living with family somewhere? Is there a shelter payment somewhere?’”

Shifting employer expectations change the borrower picture

Investors are reportedly flooding back into the office market in major urban centres like Toronto amid rising clamour from employers for their workers to spend at least a few days a week in the office.

The country’s top banks are stepping up efforts to bring back workers, while earlier this year the federal government’s Treasury Board said it was mandating a five-day office week.

The swing back toward employers’ in-office preferences, Corbitt said, is also impacting clients at renewal. “There’s a lot of back-to-work, which is biting a couple of people for sure,” she said. “I’ve had some clients call me and say, ‘I’ve been mandated back to work… I moved during COVID. How does that affect my renewal?’

“So then we discuss: Do you renew soon? Do we look at a different lender? Or do you get another job first? There’s a lot of strategies.”

First-time buyers gain ground in a sluggish market

While changing work arrangements are posing plenty of questions, one of the bright sides to a generally torrid 2026 housing market is that plenty of first-time buyers are finally finding opportunities to gain a foothold on the property ladder.

Prices have fallen across many markets amid milder competition and first-time buyers are now able to snag a property for between $500,000 and $600,000 that, Corbitt said, might have gone for $200,000 higher during the pandemic.

That price depreciation stands in stark contrast to the trend seen during the pandemic, when intense bidding wars often pushed offers well above list prices and saw many hopeful buyers overpowered in the market.

The ability to provide longer amortizations of up to 30 years is also providing extra breathing space, Corbitt added, even for buyers who could technically afford to pay on a 25-year schedule.

“We talk about the strategy of setting it at 30 years so you’re very comfortable with your payment,” she said, “and then once you’re in it, you can accelerate your payment by doing prepayments.”

But climbing interest rates are also presenting challenges for first-time buyers, while economic uncertainty has been exacerbated by the ongoing trade war with the US and rising inflation.

The cost-of-living crisis is still a real concern for many buyers, and Corbitt highlighted the reality that a high percentage of first-time entrants to the market don’t have a significant emergency fund to rely on after they’ve made their purchase.

“First-time buyers are using all their savings to get into a home,” she said. “There’s a lot of anxiety about not having any safety net to fall back on.”

Presenting a comprehensive slate of options to clients in those situations, Corbitt said, is the best way to keep them with a broker rather than defecting to a bank. “If you provide them security, then it’s not a conversation about rate,” she said.

items.title: What mortgage renewals are really costing Canadian borrowers
items.description: A new national survey surfaces the full price Canadians are paying beyond the monthly payment
items.content: <p>A new national survey surfaces the full price Canadians are paying beyond the monthly payment</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639293222322937005.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A new national survey surfaces the full price Canadians are paying beyond the monthly payment
items.body:
Rising mortgage renewal rates are hindering the financial goals of one in five Canadian Millennials and Gen X borrowers, according to new survey data that puts hard numbers to the cost pressures reshaping household finances.

The Great Delay 2026, commissioned by estate-planning platform Willful and conducted by Angus Reid Forum among 1,501 Canadian adults from September 1 to 10, found that 64% of respondents with housing payments saw those costs rise over the past year.

Nationally, 15% of Canadians identified rising mortgage renewal rates as a barrier to their financial goals, climbing to 25% among the “sandwich generation,” defined as those with at least one living parent and a child of any age.

Nearly half of that cohort, 48%, carry a mortgage, compared with 35% of Canadians overall.

“Canadians got more done with their money this year, and they still feel worse off,” said Erin Bury, CEO and co-founder of Willful.

The data arrives as brokers continue to navigate the tail end of Canada’s mortgage renewal wave, as holders of five-year terms originated at pandemic-era lows in 2020 and 2021 confront today’s substantially higher rates.

Mortgage payments squeeze household budgets

Nationally, 40% of Canadians say their position has worsened year over year, up from 37% in 2025, and 47% dipped into savings to cover everyday costs.

On average, respondents said they would need $818 more each month to reach their financial goals.

Notably, 22% of Canadians and 25% of the sandwich generation identified lower interest rates as the single change most likely to help them get there, making rate relief the second most commonly cited factor after a drop in everyday costs and inflation.

The survey’s generational mortgage data is particularly striking for brokers. Among all Canadian generations, Millennials and Gen X carry the highest mortgage rates – 45% and 47% respectively – yet represent the groups most squeezed by the renewal cycle.

Millennials face a particular bind: 45% hold a mortgage and 34% have a child under 18, making them among the most financially exposed households in the country. Only 17% have a will.

Homeownership aspirations are also being deferred, with 13% of Canadians delaying a home purchase in 2026, rising to 23% of Millennials.

The pressure is most acute within the sandwich generation. Nearly half, 48%, carry a mortgage compared with 35% of Canadians overall, and 25% cite rising mortgage renewal rates as a direct barrier to their goals, compared with 15% nationally.

With debt repayment costs up for 49% of that group against 44% of Canadians overall, 88% say they would need more monthly income to meet their goals.

Of those, 71% need at least $500 more per month, and 41% need $1,000 or more.

Lauren van den Berg, president and chief executive officer of Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) in Ottawa, drew a direct line from the data to the broker’s role.

“Renewal pressure is not just about interest rates,” she said in a Mortgage Professionals Canada survey on borrowers most exposed to payment shock.

“It is about how much room households have to absorb a higher payment. This research shows many borrowers are approaching renewal with thin payment buffers, which makes early advice, careful planning and access to the right mortgage options more important than ever.”

What brokers are hearing from renewal clients

Sarah Albert, a broker with Premiere Mortgage Centre in New Brunswick, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in August that the renewal cycle has generated a surge in refinancing as clients work to absorb higher costs.

“We have a ton of refinances right now,” Albert said.

“We’re basically resetting mortgages to 25, 30 years, consolidating some debt and actually saving them some money each month where they can kind of maintain their lifestyle.”

Albert stressed that the most effective tool for brokers navigating client renewal anxiety is direct, personal engagement – not digital workarounds.

“I have a lot of clients that are calling right now… We’re seeing a lot of panic,” she said.

“And then when they talk to us, they’re like, ‘Oh, I’m not a bad client.’ I keep saying to them, ‘You’re a better client than you think you are. You’re human. We just need to reset this and learn this lesson, and I’ve got you.’”

items.title: Laurentian Bank delists after 180 years as Fairstone deal closes
items.description: A two-part transaction reshapes Canada’s banking landscape as B2B Bank moves to Fairstone
items.content: <p>A two-part transaction reshapes Canada’s banking landscape as B2B Bank moves to Fairstone</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639002802766554708.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A two-part transaction reshapes Canada’s banking landscape as B2B Bank moves to Fairstone
items.body:
Laurentian Bank of Canada has completed its two-part sale, ending 180 years as an independent publicly listed institution and placing control in the hands of two lenders with distinct strategic goals.

The transactions, first announced in December 2025, closed November 1.

Fairstone Bank of Canada acquired all of Laurentian’s common shares at $40.50 per share, a total of approximately $1.9 billion.

National Bank of Canada (NBC) simultaneously assumed roughly $8 billion in liabilities and acquired approximately $3.7 billion in assets from Laurentian’s retail and small and medium enterprise (SME) banking portfolios, according to the joint completion announcement.

Laurentian’s common shares are expected to be delisted from the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) at market close on November 3.

What changes for the broker channel

B2B Bank, Laurentian’s broker-facing subsidiary serving approximately 27,000 financial advisers and mortgage brokers across Canada, now operates as a wholly owned subsidiary of Fairstone.

The transition extends Fairstone’s reach into broker-distributed lending, building on its standing as Canada’s largest alternative lender following the merger of Fairstone Bank and Home Trust Company completed in January 2025.

Carl De Souza, senior vice president and sector lead for North American financial institution ratings at Morningstar DBRS in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in December 2025 that Canada’s appetite for large-scale banking consolidation was nearly spent.

“There’s not much further merger and acquisition space in 2026 in the Canadian sense. I don’t know where it would come from. I think to most, the PC Financial acquisition was somewhat unexpected. So there could always be something like that. The Big Six might do some tuck-in acquisitions, but I wouldn’t say anything of a material nature,” De Souza said. 

Laurentian refocused as a commercial lender

Founded in 1846, Laurentian operated personal and commercial banking and capital markets businesses in Canada and the United States.

The restructured Laurentian will operate as a Fairstone subsidiary, concentrating on commercial real estate, inventory, and equipment financing with a particular emphasis on Québec.

“This important milestone marks the beginning of a new chapter for our organization and reinforces our position as a specialized commercial bank, allowing us to build on our strengths and focus on the areas where we can create the greatest value,” said Éric Provost, president and chief executive officer of Laurentian Bank of Canada.

Fairstone, a privately held lender with roots dating back to the 1920s, focuses on residential and commercial mortgages, consumer deposits, auto and retail financing and personal loans across more than 250 branches and digital channels. It is the parent company of mortgage market giant Home Trust.

Scott Wood, president and CEO of Fairstone Bank, said the rationale centred on diversification and scale.

“The acquisition of Laurentian Bank represents a significant step forward in the continued evolution of Fairstone Bank, enhancing the breadth and resilience of our business. Bringing together complementary businesses will diversify and scale our asset base and funding sources, support sustainable, profitable growth, and unlock opportunities to operate more effectively as we integrate our organizations,” Wood said.

For NBC, the transaction deepens its retail footprint in Québec.

“We are pleased to welcome new retail and SME clients shortly and provide them with access to National Bank’s full range of digital services, an expanded suite of financial products, our branch network and our business banking teams,” said Laurent Ferreira, president and CEO of National Bank.

National Bank was founded in 1859. It offers retail, commercial, wealth and capital markets services and reported $553 billion in assets as of July 31, 2025.

items.title: Expert: For Some, Homeownership Is Just A Dream
items.description:
For decades, buying a home was viewed as a rite of passage to adulthood. It represented stability, security, and the opportunity to build a future. Today, for many young people, it feels more like a fantasy than a realistic goal.

Recent polling and research have consistently shown that a growing number of young people no longer believe they will ever own a home. They don’t believe the housing crisis is being resolved.

While governments talk about affordability, youth do not see affordability improving in their daily lives.

Surveys of Ontarians aged 18 to 38 found that only 47% believe homeownership is achievable. More than one-quarter say it is not achievable at all, while another quarter are unsure. Young Ontarians are among the least optimistic people in Canada when it comes to their housing prospects.

A 2025 report commissioned by the Ontario Home Builders' Association found that young people in Ontario have "little hope" of buying a home. Eleven of 26 municipalities studied were deemed "completely unattainable" for middle-class households.

The report found that while house prices have more than doubled since 2005, inflation-adjusted wages have risen just 16%. In major markets such as Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, Guelph, and Barrie, homes now cost more than seven times annual pre-tax income.

Twenty-five years ago, the typical Ontario home cost roughly three to four times household income. Today, the ratio is closer to seven to nine times.

Not surprisingly, confidence has collapsed.

A housing outlook by the Ontario Real Estate Association (OREA) paints a similarly grim picture. Only 12% of Ontarians believe housing will become more affordable over the next five years. More than one-quarter of aspiring homeowners now believe they will never buy a home.

Young people are often accused of being pessimistic. In this case, however, their skepticism is justified.

This is not to say there haven’t been some positive developments.

Governments have finally acknowledged the severity of the housing crisis. The federal and Ontario governments have introduced new temporary HST rebates and other measures aimed at improving affordability while some municipalities have begun exploring reductions in development charges (DCs).

Polling conducted by Abacus Data for OREA found that 75% of Ontarians support reducing municipal DCs and 72% support provincial limits on those charges. Most reject the notion that new homebuyers should bear the cost of growth-related infrastructure.

They are right.

DCs are a hidden tax on homeownership. While municipalities defend them under the principle that "growth should pay for growth," the practical effect is that first-time buyers and young families are forced to shoulder the cost of infrastructure that benefits entire communities. The charges are embedded in housing prices and financed through mortgages.

Reducing DCs won’t solve every housing problem. But it would directly reduce construction costs, improve project viability and lower the final purchase price of homes. It would also send a signal that governments are serious about tackling affordability rather than merely talking about it.

The consequences of failing to act extend far beyond the housing market.

Housing affordability is increasingly shaping life decisions. Young adults are delaying marriage, postponing family formation, and reconsidering where they live. Some are leaving Ontario altogether in search of more affordable opportunities.

Meanwhile, there is growing evidence linking housing costs to falling birth rates. Toronto's fertility rate has fallen to just 1.11 children per woman, lower than Canada's already weak national rate of 1.25, and far below the replacement rate of 2.1. Statistics Canada has found that 37% of Canadians aged 15 to 49 do not believe they can afford to have a child within the next three years.

When housing policy begins influencing whether people can buy homes, stay in a province or have children, the issue is no longer simply about real estate. It’s a question of economic sustainability.

Young Ontarians haven’t given up on homeownership. They still want the stability and security it provides. What they have given up on is the belief that current policies are producing meaningful change.

Until governments permanently reduce the tax burden on housing and DCs, and dramatically increase supply, their skepticism will remain justified. Youth are not losing faith in homeownership. Rather, they are losing faith that governments are prepared to do what it takes to make it attainable again.

Richard Lyall is president of the Residential Construction Council of Ontario (RESCON). He has represented the building industry in Ontario since 1991. Contact him at media@rescon.com.

items.title: Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share
items.description:
Canada’s banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from the real estate bubble. Last week, the CMHC warned that the share of mortgages in arrears will climb further—especially in Ontario. The banks seem to agree, as the data shows they’ve been preparing for a sharp increase in mortgage losses. The median allowance for mortgage losses […]

The post Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian banks see more losses from delinquent mortgages in their future—a lot more losses. Mortgage loss expectations have 3x since 2019.
items.body:
Canada’s banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from the real estate bubble. Last week, the CMHC warned that the share of mortgages in arrears will climb further—especially in Ontario. The banks seem to agree, as the data shows they’ve been preparing for a sharp increase in mortgage losses. The median allowance for mortgage losses has more than doubled over the past four years.

Canadian Banks Expect Mortgage Losses To Climb Sharply

Ratio of expected credit losses to total residential mortgage balances.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Lenders need to be prepared for losses on bad loans. It doesn’t matter how much borrowers are vetted; the reality is some won’t be fully repaid. To account for this, lenders record an allowance for credit losses—an estimate of the money they do not expect to recover. It reflects expected losses, not just losses that have already occurred. Those expectations have risen sharply.

The CMHC compared each bank’s mortgage portfolio against its allowance for credit losses. The median—half of banks are better, half are worse—had an allowance equivalent to $149 per $100,000 in mortgages in Q2 2026, up 13.2% from a year earlier. That share has climbed 138.1% over the past 4 years, more than doubling. It has roughly tripled (+202.8%) since Q2 2019, back in the before times.

Keep in mind that these measure expected losses relative to mortgage balances. The banks are preparing for higher losses on each dollar lent, and they’ve lent a lot more dollars over that period. Their expectations of losses have grown alongside their mortgage portfolio over the past 7 years.

Canadian Mortgage Losses Expected To Rise Further At Some Banks

The median bank’s increase is sharp, but it hides a much sharper climb at some banks. The 75th percentile, the threshold for the top 25% of banks, saw allowances reach $337 per $100,000 in mortgages, up 47.9% from last year. The share is more than double (+126%) the median, and the highest in the data going back to 2015.

Canadian Mortgage Loss Expectations Grew At 3 In 4 Banks

Most banks expect higher mortgage losses, with roughly 3 in 4 reporting higher allowances than a year earlier. That share was just 53% a year prior, an already tenfold increase from the 5% recorded in Q2 2022. The share of banks reporting higher expected losses has gone from only 1 in 20 banks to 3 in 4 over just four years.

While the amount remains small relative to total mortgage debt, the increase is hard to ignore. Banks are preparing to lose more of each dollar lent, and more lenders expect losses to grow. That also only captures part of the rising pressure, with distress rising even faster among mortgage investment entities (MIEs).

items.title: As hopes of a Canada-US deal rise, here’s what’s at stake for housing
items.description: Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook
items.content: <p>Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639292419264737498.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook
items.body:
Formal talks between Canada and the US on a resolution to the tariff war could begin soon after prime minister Mark Carney’s Sunday social media post describing a productive recent discussion on the issue with US president Donald Trump.

Trade tensions have weighed against Canada’s economic outlook since the beginning of last year and emerged as a significant factor in the housing market’s continued malaise, pushing plenty of potential homebuyers to the sidelines and damaging consumer confidence.

While discussions between US and Canadian negotiators have yet to resume, a positive resolution to the trade war could have big implications for the national housing market.

Prospects for a 2027 recovery, some mortgage professionals say, could hinge massively on whether tariff tensions ease.

And Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) has highlighted how the trade war is worsening the mortgage strain for many borrowers in tariff-impacted parts of the country such as Southern Ontario, which has borne the brunt of US levies on steel, aluminum, automotive vehicles and parts, and agricultural products.

With homebuilding also taking a hit, the national housing agency’s deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth (pictured top) told Canadian Mortgage Professional a swift end to the trade war could potentially improve the currently dire construction outlook.

“I’m a little bit concerned on the housing supply situation that higher interest rates are affecting developers,” he said. “Now on that side, if the situation were resolved, then maybe developers would have a lot more confidence in home construction.

“From a long-term affordability [perspective], that would be positive. I think if the overall uncertainty lowered… it would give renewed confidence to people who want to go out and buy a home. If you knew the dispute was over, I think that greater certainty would help the overall economy.”

Leaders’ comments suggest potential relief for borrowers ahead

Last week, Trump told a rally in Michigan that the trade war could be settled “pretty soon,” as he stepped up campaigning ahead of the crucial midterm elections, set to take place on November 3.

Trump and Carney’s recent statements mark the first hint of a possible détente since an end to tariff negotiations in August triggered a sudden escalation in the trade war.   

Ab Iorwerth said the ongoing trade war is part of the reason mortgage strain seems worse in Southern Ontario than other parts of the country, even though there’s no sign of a wider mortgage meltdown caused by rising arrears.

“There’s a lot of protection within the system so I don’t think we’re looking at a systemic issue, but there’s a lot of people being adversely impacted by what’s happening to them individually,” he said. “And I think a lot of households are facing challenges with these higher interest rates that they’re bearing and the uncertainty over the trajectory of mortgage rates.

“There’s still that lingering concern over inflation and then there’s uncertainty on the macroeconomic front with trade. So I think all of this is creating a lot of stress for individual households about what might happen.”

Iran and inflation add further complications for housing

While tariffs were the defining story of 2025 for the Canadian economy, they’ve been joined this year by surging fuel prices because of the war in Iran – another curveball that could complicate the picture even if the trade war ends.

Those higher fuel prices have sparked fears of a wider spillover into headline inflation, one of the main reasons the Bank of Canada opted to hike its benchmark interest rate last week for the first time in over three years.

Against that backdrop, the central bank doesn’t see the housing market bouncing back in 2027 – although it underlined the positive effects an end to the trade war could potentially have.

A Canada-US deal reducing tariffs “would increase exports and business investment, boosting employment and incomes,” the BoC said in its latest Monetary Policy Report. “Higher demand could increase the pass-through from higher energy prices. The removal of counter-tariffs would provide an offset.”

items.content: <p>Haventree’s COO talks lending trends and the ever-evolving Canadian borrower</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639292444699523088.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Haventree’s COO talks lending trends and the ever-evolving Canadian borrower
items.body:
The alternative lending space is changing – and as the big banks continue tightening their lending criteria, alt lenders are seeing their market share grow. At MortgageFest, we caught up with Haventree Bank chief operating officer Joe Cote to hear his thoughts on current trends and what’s in store for the sector down the line.

[00:00] There's not a very simple straightforward borrower type anymore. We're talking about great credit scores that are well into the 700s, low 800s, but we're talking about life happens. Brokers are small business owners. This affordability issue has now compounded for 5 years and the alternative space is going to be, I think, a huge eye-opener for a lot of the brokers.

[00:30] Fergal McAlinden: All right. So, next up we have Joe Cote, Chief Operating Officer at HipBilt Bank, whose booth we see just over here. Have you been having many productive conversations with brokers today?

[00:40] Joe Cote: Lots of discussions. I certainly think that there's been a lot of changes throughout the industry, specifically with HipBilt, which is very exciting. And having a lot of brokers come back and are interested to see, you know, tell me more. Tell me what you're doing. We're hearing a lot of exciting things that have been happening over the course of the last 6 to 12 months. Tell me what's happening over the course of the next 6 to 12 months and how can we partner together?

[01:00] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And the event is happening at a really interesting time for the industry. I mean, not that we haven't had any non-eventful times over the past few years. It's just been one thing after the next. But 2026, how are you assessing the market this year? How's it been?

[01:13] Joe Cote: I think obviously the market has had a fairly large impact on a lot of brokers and a lot of lenders, the community at large. We are still very happy and fortunate with our position and our performance so far this year. We've got great partners. I think that value proposition that we have certainly been working on has been what, the proof in the pudding of being able to look to those partners. We've got a lot of partners that have come back. I think that they're very excited with the service, the products, and the relationships that we've built. And from an overall performance standpoint, we're going to finish the year actually fairly strong and we got some good growth prospects for 2027.

[01:45] Fergal McAlinden: I was interested to hear, Joe, from lenders about borrower types. We know that they've evolved a lot over the past few years. I'm wondering if there's a specific type of borrower that you feel best placed to cater to in the current market.

[01:57] Joe Cote: I think the short answer to that is there's not a very simple straightforward borrower type anymore. Well, I think one of the opportunities has certainly been around the evolution of the alt space and how it's very much part of the prime offering now. And it used to be around bruised credit, which is still very much the case and will always be part of the ideal client profile that the alt space was built off of.

[02:18] But now we look at the tightening credit box from a lot of the larger Schedule 1 banks. That business flow, as it's been tightening, has actually been coming into the alternative space. And that's not necessarily a bad thing. We're talking about great credit scores that are well into the 700s, low 800s. But we're talking about life happens. We're talking about divorces. We're talking about CRA. Multiple properties, business for self.

[02:43] It doesn't necessarily mean bruised credit anymore. It just means maybe not as simple from a credit profile standpoint. So, we are truly running the entire gamut of what I would say is the alternative space is now alt A through to what was bruised credit before. And I'd love to see the evolution of the space and the value that we're bringing back to the Canadian consumers.

[03:04] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And I think that evolution, nobody's expecting that to slow anytime soon, especially with how the market is this year and some of the challenges being faced by buyers. When it comes to brokers, how have you been dealing with them this year? Are there any kind of approaches you've been keeping in mind with brokers?

[03:19] Joe Cote: Yeah, a big emphasis of our partnership model with brokers has been, how do we just focus on building our processes, our expectations, our interaction models completely around the broker community. And thinking about brokers as small business owners.

[03:34] I've been saying this a lot just recently on stage. I think the biggest thing was around brokers are small business owners. It is all about the experience. It's about the referral business. And if they land a great client experience based on the partnership that they have with the lender, that client's going to come back. They're going to refer more business.

[03:52] And that alternative space, again, especially in the small business community and or gig economy, we've got so many borrowers that are looking for solutions that they didn't even know existed before. So, we've basically repositioned, I would say, a lot of our processes and policies to be built around brokers and the client experience, keeping that really at heart.

[04:10] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Looking ahead, 2027, hard as it is to believe, is just around the corner. Any trends that you're keeping an eye on or anything that you're expecting to be a big factor next year?

[04:20] Joe Cote: It's too fast. I miss summer already. I would say the trend, if anything, is probably going to be continuing. If you think about it, a couple of things. One has been the compounding effect of the interest rate environment, the tariffs, both in terms of just cost of goods as well as taxation on it, especially for small business owners.

[04:40] All those financing needs actually aren't going away. The financing needs are going to increase, especially if you think about this affordability issue has now compounded for 5 years. That's taxing a lot of Canadians, and that problem's not going to get any easier in the current environment.

[04:56] Not only what's happening with Canada and the US, but certainly I think in terms of the interest rate environment over the course of the next 12 months, there's not a single person that's expecting interest rates to stay flat. In that increasing environment, it's going to only compound the problem, and brokers are going to need to understand that business model.

[05:15] They're going to need to find ways to actually support their clients who are going to have needs, and knowing full well that the traditional means of prime sourcing is not necessarily going to be as viable as it used to be historically. And the alternative space is going to be, I think, a huge eye-opener for a lot of the brokers that are not currently accessing the alt space like they should be.

[05:27] Fergal McAlinden: For sure, and on that rate question, as you mentioned, I think we're all just strapped in waiting to see what happens on the bond market and on trade war and everything.

[05:34] Joe Cote: Yeah.

[05:34] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah, the only thing that's certain is that we have more uncertainty ahead, I think, is the way to put it. Maybe just one last word on the event, Joe. Have you met your target audience, and we'll be seeing you next year?

[05:43] Joe Cote: Absolutely. It's been wonderful, actually. Not only have I met, from an audience perspective, everybody in terms of our partners, as well as potential net new partners, both in terms of brokers, as well as a lot of other broker ancillary partners here.

[05:58] I think about the technology providers, I think about net new products that are coming on the market. I can point to a couple over there, which I just think are phenomenal in terms of the innovation that is showcased at the event, and I love being part of it, hearing the stories, how we can better service our clients.

[06:12] And looking at these partner solutions on how we can kind of improve the experience, I will definitely be back.

[06:15] Fergal McAlinden: Love to hear it. Okay, great stuff. Thank you for stopping by. Much appreciated. Then enjoy the rest of the event.

[06:19] Joe Cote: Thanks for having me.
